mesoscaleDiscussions.summary: The risk of strong to severe downbursts will continue for another hour or two

details.label: Summary
details.text: The risk of strong to severe downbursts will continue for another hour or two

details.label: Discussion
details.text: The latest radar data from KDGX depicts outflow-dominant thunderstorms, with new cell development along outflow boundaries. The JAN 00Z sounding sampled steep low-level lapse rates and moderate-strong surface-based buoyancy, and despite weak deep-layer flow/shear, this environment remains favorable for strong to severe downbursts. Given the overall lack of convective organization, the severe risk should gradually diminish over the next couple hours as the boundary layer nocturnally cools

details.text: MOST PROBABLE PEAK WIND GUST...55-70 MPH

mesoscaleDiscussions.summary: Severe hail remains a concern with the stronger sustained supercells this evening

details.label: Summary
details.text: Severe hail remains a concern with the stronger sustained supercells this evening

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Multiple sustained supercells have progressed across central MN over the past few hours, with marginally severe hail reported (particularly with the storms over northern MN). 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE remains in place, along with 35-40 kts of effective bulk shear per 00Z mesoanalysis. The 00Z MPX observed sounding also shows a hodograph with appreciable low-level curvature and modest elongation, suggesting that supercells will remain the dominant mode of the convection through the evening hours. Large hail should remain the primary threat, though a damaging gust or tornado cannot be ruled out

details.label: Summary
details.text: The risk of damaging wind gusts should increase over the next few hours. While a watch is not currently expected, trends will be monitored

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Isolated thunderstorms are evolving within a zone of broad low-level confluence extending from parts of Middle/western TN into far northern MS. Over the next few hours, increasing large-scale ascent preceding a midlevel wave moving across the lower OH Valley could support an increase in thunderstorm coverage within this zone. Ahead of this activity, a warm and very moist PBL (upper 70s to near 80 dewpoints) are yielding a corridor of strong surface-based buoyancy. While modest deep-layer flow/shear and lack of a LLJ should tend to limit convective organization, some strengthening of midlevel northwesterly flow accompanying the midlevel wave (sampled by upstream VWP) could favor a loosely organized cluster of storms. If this evolution occurs, damaging wind gusts will be the primary concern. While a gradual increase in nocturnal static stability and the modest deep-layer shear may temper the overall severe risk, convective trends will be monitored
